statements: The chief issue is an incidentally characterized small hepatic nodule in a 50-year-old woman with chronic mild right upper quadrant pain.
Her own concern is abdominal pain.
The clinically important problem is determining the nature of the 17 mm liver lesion.
Salient positive findings are the imaging characteristics.
Ultrasound showed a 15 mm homogeneous hyperechoic nodule in segment VI.
MRI showed a well-circumscribed 17 mm lesion.
The lesion was moderately T2 hyperintense.
The lesion was T1 hypointense.
The lesion was hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging with ADC restriction.
The lesion demonstrated arterial-phase hyperenhancement.
The lesion showed washout on portal/delayed phases.
The lesion showed capsule enhancement.
There was signal drop on opposed-phase imaging.
The signal drop on opposed-phase imaging indicated intralesional fat.
These are classic malignant-appearing dynamic enhancement features.
The combination of arterial enhancement plus washout plus capsule is especially characteristic of malignant-appearing dynamic enhancement features.
The lesion is small.
The lesion is solitary.
Relevant background findings are notable mainly for the absence of chronic liver disease risk factors.
The patient has no past medical history.
The patient has normal CBC and liver function tests.
The patient has normal alpha-fetoprotein.
The patient has negative hepatitis B serologies.
The patient has negative hepatitis C serologies.
Physical examination was unremarkable.
She is a non-smoker.
These findings make common cirrhosis-related hepatocellular carcinoma less expected.
These findings do not exclude hepatocellular carcinoma.
Certain variants of hepatocellular carcinoma can occur in non-cirrhotic liver.
Pertinent negatives help with the differential.
There is no evidence provided of cirrhosis.
There is no evidence provided of viral hepatitis.
There is no evidence provided of elevated AFP.
There is no evidence provided of systemic illness.
The lesion is not described as having peripheral nodular discontinuous enhancement.
The lesion is not described as having progressive fill-in expected for hemangioma.
The lesion is not described as having a central scar.
The lesion is not described as having the typical enhancement pattern of focal nodular hyperplasia.
The presence of washout and capsule enhancement argues strongly against benign lesions such as focal fatty change, hemangioma, or most adenomas.
Metastatic disease is less supported.
There is no known primary malignancy.
The lesion contains fat.
Fat is more characteristic of hepatocellular neoplasms than most metastases.
Hepatocellular carcinoma fits best.
The lesion shows arterial-phase hyperenhancement.
The lesion shows portal/delayed washout.
The lesion shows capsule enhancement.
These features together are hallmark imaging features of hepatocellular carcinoma.
Intralesional fat can be seen in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Intralesional fat can be seen especially in small or well-differentiated tumors.
Diffusion restriction also supports malignancy.
Hepatocellular adenoma is plausible.
Adenomas can occur in non-cirrhotic livers.
Adenomas may contain fat with T1/T2 signal changes.
Adenomas more often show arterial enhancement without the classic combination of washout and enhancing capsule seen here.
Diffusion restriction is less typical for adenoma.
No risk factors such as oral contraceptive use, obesity, or metabolic syndrome are provided.
Focal nodular hyperplasia is less likely.
Focal nodular hyperplasia can occur in women without liver disease.
Focal nodular hyperplasia usually shows arterial hyperenhancement with persistent enhancement rather than washout.
Focal nodular hyperplasia often has a central scar.
Focal nodular hyperplasia typically does not show capsule enhancement or diffusion restriction.
Hepatic angiomyolipoma could contain fat and be hypervascular.
Hepatic angiomyolipoma is uncommon.
The classic HCC-like washout/capsule pattern makes hepatic angiomyolipoma less likely.
Hemangioma is unlikely.
The lesion is hyperechoic on ultrasound.
MRI behavior is not typical for hemangioma.
Hemangiomas usually show very high T2 signal.
Hemangiomas usually show peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in.
Hemangiomas do not usually show washout and capsule.
Despite the absence of cirrhosis, hepatitis, or AFP elevation, the MRI pattern is most decisive.
Arterial hyperenhancement plus washout plus capsule enhancement in a fat-containing hepatic lesion with diffusion restriction is most consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma.
In a non-cirrhotic liver and with fat content, a steatohepatitic or well-differentiated HCC phenotype would be compatible.
The single best diagnosis from the provided data is hepatocellular carcinoma.
The differential diagnosis includes hepatocellular carcinoma with high likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes hepatocellular adenoma with medium likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes focal nodular hyperplasia with low likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes hepatic angiomyolipoma with low likelihood.
The differential diagnosis includes hemangioma with low likelihood.
The final diagnosis is hepatocellular carcinoma.
